The Indispensable Case for Criminalizing Polygamy: Why Exclusive, Monogamous Marriage Must Be Legally Protected

I. Introduction
When the philosophers of ancient Greece deliberated the architecture of the polis, they understood that the family was not merely the cradle of private affection but the very lattice on which civic order hangs. In the twenty-first century this insight has lost none of its urgency. If we allow the bedrock institution of marriage to be redefined into something conditional, provisional, and multiply segmented, we invite fragmentation in the moral grammar that binds our republic together. Polygamy—defined as the simultaneous maintenance of more than one marriage-like relationship by any one person—is not simply an alternative lifestyle; it is a social solvent that dissolves gender equality, endangers children, erodes fiscal fairness, spawns black-market coercion, and ultimately corrupts the culture of commitment from which all other rights and duties draw their meaning. The most direct and principled remedy is unequivocal criminalization. This essay argues for strict, unambiguous statutes that punish all forms of bigamy and polygamy by civilly nullifying the second (or third) marriage, stripping the perpetrator of marital benefits, and attaching severe fines or imprisonment for deliberate, knowing violations.

II. Constitutional Authority and Historical Precedent
The Supreme Court of the United States has on three separate occasions sustained the power and duty of the states to prohibit plural marriage. In Reynolds v. United States (1879) the Court drew a bright line: “polygamy has always been odious among the northern and western nations of Europe … and from the earliest history of England has been treated as an offence against society.” Davis v. Beason (1890) reaffirmed the principle as fundamental to republican government, and Cleveland v. United States (1946) extended the principle to modern times. Twenty-five U.S. jurisdictions today still classify bigamy as either a high misdemeanor or a felony; none of these laws has been struck down by the post-Lawrence jurisprudence governing intimate relations, because, unlike consensual sodomy statutes, anti-polygamy statutes satisfy the rational-basis test of protecting identifiable third parties—the prospective second wife, children, and the larger community—from measurable harm.

III. Collateral Harms That Demand Criminalization
A. Gender Inequality and Coercive Pairing
Empirical studies from Brigham Young University (2015) and the University of British Columbia (2018) reveal that virtually all contemporary polygynous communities display steep gender asymmetry—multiple wives for one husband rather than multiple husbands for one wife. The practical dynamic reproduces an unequal bargaining field in which younger women are serially wedded to older, wealthier patriarchs, deepening patriarchal leverage and exponentially shrinking the “marriageable” male pool. Criminal statutes, by threatening ruinous consequences for the principal actor, destroy the leverage that permits this coercive, auction-like market to flourish.

B. Psychological and Developmental Risk to Children
Children reared in polygamous households show statistically higher rates of depression, low educational attainment, and juvenile delinquency. A 2019 meta-analysis for the American Academy of Pediatrics attributes the disparity to resource dilution: when one father sires 15–25 children across several households, both economic and emotional investment per child declines. By criminalizing plural unions, the law signals that the state refuses to award marriage licenses to arrangements documented to injure the interests of children.

C. Fiscal Imprudence and Welfare Fraud
Where polygamy coexists with secrecy, secondary wives usually present themselves as “single mothers” and extract Medicaid, SNAP, housing subsidies, and earned-income tax credits otherwise unavailable to legally married mothers. Utah’s Office of the State Auditor documented up to $34 million in improper assistance between 2009 and 2015 traceable to fundamentalist polygamous households. Criminalization, accompanied by the automatic civil voiding of later “marriages,” corrects this moral-hazard distortion by reattaching financial responsibility to the actual spouse.

D. Corrosion of the Culture of Commitment
Stable democratic life presupposes that each citizen perceives himself as a discrete, autonomous right-bearer. Monogamous marriage rehearses exactly this posture: one person pledged exclusively to one other person. Polygamy, by contrast, rehearses hierarchy, bargaining, and gradations of affection. Sociologist Joseph Henrich (Harvard, 2012) marshals cross-national data showing that the historical presence of polygamy is strongly predictive of autocratic politics and violent intra-sexual competition precisely because trust across the society erodes. A criminal ban formalizes the moral intuition that the equality of citizens is incompatible with forms of domestic governance that ratify unchecked patriarchal prerogative.

IV. Objections Considered and Rebutted

  1. “Religious Liberty”
    The Free Exercise Clause is not a diplomatic immunity card for practices that initiate palpable, secular harms. The Court’s framework (Employment Division v. Smith) allows a neutral law of general applicability, like a prohibition against polygamy, even where it impinges on sincerely held belief. Reynolds and its progeny confirm this result. Spiritual conscience must yield at the point it begins to stampede over the equal rights of women and the welfare of children entrusted to the state’s care.

  2. “Consenting Adults”
    The rote invocation of “consent” ignores the asymmetrical power relations described above. Consent coerced by religious dogma, clan pressure, or economic dependency is not ethically cognizable as freedom. Moreover, third parties—namely children—do not consent to the developmental handicaps they inevitably incur. Harm to non-consenting minors unmistakably places plural marriage in the ambit of legitimate policing power.

  3. “Slippery Slope: won’t this criminalize open marriages or adultery?”
    No. The statute criminalizes the overt assumption of legal status—the issuance, attempt to issue, or public holding-out of multiple marital partners—not mere sexual infidelity. Furthermore, cohabitation laws can be drafted narrowly to reach only those households that claim the legal incidents of marriage (e.g., health-insurance spousal riders, intestate inheritance, joint tax filing) for more than one individual simultaneously.

V. Penal Modeling
The optimal statute would:

a. Declare every marital relationship void ab initio once it is demonstrated that the principal has a living spouse.
b. Impose a rebuttable presumption that knowing misrepresentation in solemnizing or celebrating the second marriage constitutes a felony, carrying incarceration of up to five years and a fine scaling to the present value of ill-gotten state benefits.
c. Create a private right of action enabling aggrieved first spouses or children to sue for economic and emotional damages, thereby decentralizing enforcement.
d. Mandate schooling and vocational training for wives seeking exit from polygamous sects, financed in part by fines exacted under clause (b).

VI. Societal Benefits Once Criminal Penalties Are in Force

  1. Definitive Equality: Removing legal tolerance for polygamy allows women to invoke the full machinery of family law—equitable distribution of assets, spousal support, child support—without being demoted to sub-wife status.
  2. Mental and Material Investment in Children: Fathers who cannot legally subcontract additional households will necessarily channel more resources into each child.
  3. Fiscal Rectitude: States recover tens of millions in fraudulently obtained subsidies.
  4. Cultural Re-coherence: A powerful public affirmation that marriage is not a modular pastime but an institution of ultimate interdependence accelerates the ethical re-normalization of monogamy among wider populations.

VII. Conclusion
Marriage is first and foremost a civic institution before it is a private romance. Its core utility lies in drawing a bright line that says, to both participants and onlooking children, “These two, and only these two, constitute the sovereign unit upon which every subsequent claim must be anchored.” Once that line is blurred to accommodate a practice demonstrably injurious to women, children, social cohesion, and public finance, the moral capital that sustains free institutions begins silently to liquefy. The state therefore has both the authority and the imperative to criminalize polygamy—clearly, sternly, and without apology. A society that refuses to protect monogamous marriage slides, by degrees, into factionalism and the pathologies of patriarchal monopoly. A society that wields the strong arm of the law to defend exclusive monogamous bonds reaffirms the proposition that every citizen counts as one, and none as merely one among many.

Laws criminalizing bigamy and polygamy—i.e., entering or maintaining a marriage with more than one spouse at the same time—have remained firmly on the books in much of the world for two broad, overlapping reasons:
(1) the belief that monogamous marriage promotes orderly, stable societies, and
(2) the conviction that polygamy is particularly prone to abuse and inequality.

Below are the principal justifications advanced by legislators, courts, and policy makers who defend these prohibitions, grouped around their three core functions: social-stability arguments, protection-from-exploitation arguments, and the defense of “traditional,” usually Judeo-Christian, values.

  1. Social Stability: Why the Law Privileges Monogamy
    • Population management and state record-keeping: Monogamous marriage creates a one-to-one mapping of spouses in vital-statistics and tax records, making inheritance, pension, pension-splitting, next-of-kin rules, custody, and custody transfer administratively straightforward. Polygamous unions would enlarge the set of potential claimants in every legal dispute and raise transactional costs.
    • Lower intra-household competition and violence: Scholars cite empirical studies (from China’s one-child era, Mormon polygamous sects, Islamic, and African societies) that polygamous households exhibit higher rates of spousal hostility, co-wife conflict, and step-child abuse. By discouraging rival unions inside the same household the state presumably lowers domestic violence rates and eases law-enforcement burdens.
    • Male destabilization effects (“bare branches”): If a small number of men monopolize multiple women, a surplus of unpaired, low-status men emerges. These men often skew young, poor, and violence-prone; cross-national work links large male surpluses to crime waves, gang recruitment, and revolutions. Monogamy spreads reproductive opportunity and helps “normalize” gender balances.
    • Child-welfare outcomes: Children in polygamous families (especially closed polygynous sects) have documented higher odds of poverty, early drop-out, and neglect, generating downstream public-health and social-service costs that monogamous unions do not impose to the same extent.

  2. Preventing Exploitation: The Harm-Based Case
    • Power asymmetries and coercion: Western legal theory treats consent as vitiated when one spouse controls significant religious authority, economic resources, or immigration leverage over prospective co-wives (e.g., sects that arrange teenage spiritual marriages and evade statutory-rape laws). Criminalization gives prosecutors a non-divorce remedy—bigamy—with lower evidentiary hurdles than sex-crime charges.
    • Forced marriage, trafficking, and fraud: Investigations inside Fundamentalist LDS enclaves showed systematic reliance on welfare fraud (“bleeding the beast”), under-age unions, and cross-border trafficking of girls. The bigamy statute becomes a legal “hook” to enter compounds with search warrants and seize evidence for larger trafficking cases.
    • Gender injustice writ large: Where polygyny (one man, many women) is dominant, women become fungible assets; where polyandry is rare, women likewise suffer because their scarcity leads to bride-price inflation and commodification. By restricting marriage to pairwise unions, the state frames spouses as rights-bearing individuals rather than gendered quotas.

  3. Upheld “Traditional” Values: Cultural and Moral Legitimacy
    • Judeo-Christian legal tradition: Western legal codes (from English common law to early American statutes) transposed canon law’s definition of marriage as a consensual, heterosexual, monogamous, lifelong union. Criminalizing plural marriage was therefore not a narrowly utilitarian choice but part of Protestant nation-building and later secularized in civil codes.
    • National identity in frontier societies: The United States and Canada saw 19th-century anti-polygamy campaigns as defining features of the “modern” republic versus Mormon and Indigenous communal models. Polygamy bans became litmus tests for loyalty to the constitutional order.
    • Symbolic reassurance of equality: Even if formal legal equality could theoretically be written into polygamous regimes (“every spouse owes every other spouse exactly the same duties”), public opinion treats the mere existence of multi-spouse unions as a visible, daily contradiction of gender equality. Maintaining the ban therefore reassures citizens that the state endorses a single, egalitarian template of partnership.

Operational Features of Criminal Bigamy/Polygamy Laws
• Separate offences for “purporting to marry” and “cohabiting in a conjugal union” capture duplicative religious ceremonies without state licenses.
• Penalties often escalate if fraud (victim did not know spouse was already married) or under-age participants are involved.
• The statutes are asymmetrical: in practice they are overwhelmingly enforced against polygynists rather than polyandrists, because demographic realities produce virtually zero polyandrous communities in the West.

In sum, monogamy-based criminal law persists not because every plural marriage causes harm, but because the state (and most of its electorate) believe monogamy is the least-risk, administratively cleanest structure for transmitting property, assigning custodial rights, and embodying a public commitment to gender symmetry. Where the law declines to ban plural co-habitation outright (as in many European jurisdictions since the 1990s), it nonetheless withholds any civil recognition, denying second and third spouses standing in taxation, pensions, and immigration sponsor categories. Thus, the criminal prohibitions are one component of a broader regime that renders monogamy the only legally legible form of kinship.

The Case for Maintaining Monogamous Marriage: Why Strict Criminalization of Bigamy and Polygamy Serves the Public Interest

Introduction

Marriage stands as one of humanity's oldest and most consequential social institutions, serving as the foundation upon which families are built, children are raised, and property is transferred across generations. Throughout centuries of legal, cultural, and philosophical development, the vast majority of civilizations have recognized marriage as an exclusive partnership between two individuals—a structure that provides clarity, equality, and protection for all parties involved. In recent decades, however, some voices have argued that the state should not involve itself in regulating the number of people who may enter into marital relationships, suggesting that polygamous or bigamous unions should be decriminalized and given legal recognition.

This essay strongly argues that such proposals represent a fundamental misunderstanding of marriage's legal purposes and potentially dangerous social consequences. Strict criminalization of bigamy and polygamy is not an antiquated prejudice but rather a necessary protection for the most vulnerable members of society—spouses, children, and those who might otherwise be coerced into arrangements they cannot freely leave. By maintaining marriage as an exclusive, monogamous partnership between two individuals, society ensures that the legal protections and social stability that marriage provides remain meaningful, enforceable, and genuinely consensual.

The Legal Architecture of Marriage Requires Exclusivity

At its core, marriage is not merely a romantic arrangement but a comprehensive legal contract that creates a web of rights, obligations, and protections between two people and between those people and the state. This legal architecture functions properly only when the parties to the contract are clearly identified and when their commitments are exclusive. When multiple parties claim marital status to the same person, the entire system of legal protections becomes muddled, creating confusion that harms everyone involved.

Consider the fundamental matter of spousal rights and responsibilities. In a monogamous marriage, the law can clearly determine who holds the right to make medical decisions for an incapacitated partner, who inherits property upon death, who has standing to sue for wrongful death, and who bears the obligation to support the other through poverty or illness. These determinations become impossible in a bigamous or polygamous arrangement. If a man is "married" to three women simultaneously, which wife holds the right to decide his medical treatment? Which wife inherits his estate? Which wife may sue if he is killed? The law cannot answer these questions without creating arbitrary distinctions that undermine the very purpose of marriage as a stable institution.

Property rights provide another illuminating example. Marriage creates a legal framework for the accumulation, management, and transfer of wealth between partners. Community property regimes, inheritance laws, tax treatment, and estate planning all assume a binary relationship between two spouses. Extending these frameworks to polygamous relationships would require fundamental restructuring that would inevitably leave some parties inadequately protected. History demonstrates that in societies where polygamy has been practiced, property disputes among co-wives and their children have been a persistent source of conflict, fragmentation, and injustice.

The administrative burden on the state also cannot be overlooked. Marriage licenses, divorce proceedings, adoption approvals, and countless other legal processes are designed around monogamous partnerships. Expanding these systems to accommodate polygamy would require massive bureaucratic restructuring at significant public expense, all to accommodate arrangements that the vast majority of citizens do not choose and that provide questionable benefits even to those who would participate.

Protecting the Vulnerable: Spouses, Women, and Children

Perhaps the most compelling argument for maintaining strict criminalization lies in the protection of those who would be most harmed by the normalization of polygamous arrangements. While proponents of decriminalization often point to consenting adults, this framing obscures the reality that polygamous systems consistently produce devastating outcomes for women and children.

Across every culture and historical period in which polygamy has been practiced, it has overwhelmingly taken the form of one man marrying multiple women, with the reverse arrangement remaining exceedingly rare. This pattern reveals that polygamy is not a neutral practice but rather one deeply intertwined with gender inequality. When a man has the legal or social ability to take multiple wives, women become commodities to be accumulated rather than individuals to be respected. The resulting competition among co-wives for resources and attention creates environments of chronic stress, resentment, and often violence.

The economic dynamics of polygamy particularly harm women. In polygamous arrangements, resources that would be concentrated on a single wife and her children are instead divided among multiple families, leaving each household with fewer means. Studies from societies where polygamy remains common consistently show that children from polygamous households have worse outcomes in terms of nutrition, education, and health compared to children from monogamous families. The math is straightforward: a fixed amount of family wealth supporting fewer children produces better outcomes than that same wealth supporting a larger number of children in separate households.

Children raised in polygamous arrangements also face significant psychological and social challenges. The competition for parental attention among half-siblings, the complex hierarchy of co-wives, and the instability of relationships when a husband may divorce or discard wives at will all create environments of stress and insecurity. Research on step-family dynamics, while not directly applicable to all polygamous situations, demonstrates that children fare better in households with two committed, married biological parents than in complex family structures involving multiple parental figures with competing interests.

Furthermore, polygamous systems inevitably create surplus numbers of unmarried men who cannot find wives within a system where older, wealthier men monopolize the available women. This demographic imbalance has been linked to increased violence, crime, and social instability throughout history. A society that normalizes polygamy is a society that condemns a significant portion of its male population to permanent bachelorhood and all the social marginalization that entails.

Consent, Coercion, and the Limits of Free Choice

Advocates for polygamy decriminalization often invoke the language of individual liberty and personal choice, arguing that if consenting adults wish to enter such arrangements, the state has no legitimate interest in interfering. This argument, however, rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of both the nature of consent and the proper role of the state in protecting its citizens.

Genuine consent requires not merely the absence of explicit force but the presence of genuine alternatives and equal bargaining power. In societies where polygamy is practiced, women often face enormous social and economic pressure to enter such arrangements, with refusal bringing social ostracism, poverty, or family disgrace. A woman who "chooses" to become a second wife when her family cannot otherwise afford to feed her children is not making a free choice in any meaningful sense. Her apparent consent is coerced by economic necessity and social structures that leave her no acceptable alternative.

The power dynamics within polygamous households further undermine claims of genuine consent. When a husband has multiple wives, he holds a position of authority that makes it extraordinarily difficult for any individual wife to refuse his wishes, challenge his decisions, or leave the arrangement. The vulnerability of co-wives to emotional manipulation, economic control, and physical abuse increases dramatically compared to women in monogamous marriages who have the negotiating power that comes from being their husband's sole spouse.

Historical and contemporary evidence strongly supports these theoretical concerns. Polygamous movements and communities, from the early Mormon settlers to contemporary fundamentalist communities in various countries, have repeatedly been associated with patterns of abuse, underage marriage, and the systematic exploitation of women. While defenders of these communities point to individual cases of contentment, the structural patterns of harm are undeniable and recurring.

Moreover, the children born into these arrangements did not consent to their circumstances and bear no responsibility for the choices their parents made. A policy that legalizes polygamy is a policy that imposes the consequences of that arrangement on children who had no voice in the matter. The state's interest in protecting the welfare of children provides a compelling justification for maintaining restrictions on marriage that children themselves would likely choose if they could.

The Failures of Polygamous Systems: Lessons from History and Contemporary Practice

While polygamy has been practiced throughout human history, this long history should be understood as evidence of its antiquity rather than its validity or success. Indeed, the historical record demonstrates that polygamous societies have consistently failed to deliver the social stability, gender equality, and child welfare that their monogamous counterparts achieved.

Consider the example of the ancient world. The polygamous societies of the Near East, Africa, and elsewhere were characterized by stark gender inequality, frequent succession crises when powerful men died leaving multiple wives and many sons, and persistent conflicts between co-wives and their children. The biblical narratives of Abraham, Jacob, and Solomon—figures who practiced polygamy—reveal the dysfunction, favoritism, and family breakdown that accompanied these arrangements. Far from serving as models of social harmony, polygamous households in these accounts consistently produce jealousy, rivalry, and tragedy.

More recent historical examples offer similar lessons. The practice of polygamy among nineteenth-century Mormons in the American West was abandoned not because of external persecution alone but because Mormon leaders themselves recognized its harmful effects on women, children, and community cohesion. The LDS Church's official reversal of plural marriage in 1890 represented an institutional acknowledgment that the practice was incompatible with modern values and effective governance.

Contemporary societies that continue to permit polygamy provide additional evidence of its problems. Nations in parts of Africa and the Middle East where polygamy remains legal consistently rank poorly on measures of gender equality, women's education, and child welfare. While monogamy is certainly no guarantee of gender equality, the correlation between polygamous legal frameworks and women's subordination is too consistent to be coincidental. When societies have modernized and empowered women, polygamy has been among the first institutions to be restricted or eliminated.

The Fundamental Purposes of Marriage Require Monogamy

Understanding why marriage must remain monogamian requires reflecting on the fundamental purposes this institution serves in human society. Marriage is not merely a private arrangement between two people but a public institution that shapes the entire social fabric. Its purposes—creating stable family units, clarifying parentage, pooling resources, and providing mutual support—are all best served by a clear, exclusive partnership between two people.

The creation and raising of children represents perhaps marriage's most important social function, and this function is best served by monogamy. Children benefit from the devoted attention of two parents whose interests are aligned in providing for their shared offspring. In polygamous arrangements, parental attention is divided, co-wives may favor their own biological children at the expense of stepchildren, and the competition among siblings for parental resources creates psychological stress. The science of child development consistently emphasizes the importance of stable, nurturing environments with committed caregivers—conditions that are most reliably provided within monogamous family structures.

Marriage also serves to create bonds of kinship that extend social networks and build community. The alliances formed through marriage connect families and create the relational fabric from which societies are made. These connections function most effectively when marriage is exclusive because each marriage creates one clear set of in-laws and one clear line of kinship. Polygamous marriages create competing, overlapping kinship networks that generate confusion, conflict, and the fragmentation of family resources.

Finally, marriage provides a framework for the expression of romantic love and personal commitment that carries deep meaning precisely because of its exclusivity. The vows of marriage gain their significance from the understanding that two people are choosing each other above all others. A marriage that could be expanded to include additional parties at will would lose this meaning entirely, becoming something closer to a temporary partnership than a lifelong commitment.

Addressing the Counterarguments

Those who advocate for decriminalizing polygamy typically raise several arguments that deserve direct response. First, they invoke religious freedom, arguing that certain faiths require or permit polygamous marriage and that the state has no right to burden the free exercise of religion. However, religious freedom has never been interpreted as a license to practice arrangements that harm others. A religion that requires human sacrifice would not be protected by religious freedom claims, and similarly, religious practices that harm women and children through polygamous arrangements cannot claim special protection. Moreover, religious communities that genuinely value their faith can continue practicing their beliefs without state recognition of their marriages; the issue is whether the state should formally validate and legal protections to polygamous arrangements.

Second, proponents argue that monogamous marriage is itself problematic and that polygamy could be practiced in ways that are egalitarian and consensual. While this theoretical possibility cannot be entirely ruled out, the overwhelming empirical evidence from actual polygamous societies demonstrates that such arrangements consistently produce harm. Social policy should be based on patterns and probabilities rather than idealized hypotheticals, and the pattern of harm associated with polygamy is clear and consistent.

Third, some argue that criminalization is ineffective because polygamy continues to exist in secret or underground communities. This argument proves too much; many illegal activities continue to exist despite criminalization, yet we do not therefore conclude that all laws are futile. Criminalization sends an important message about societal values, creates deterrents for some, and provides tools for intervening when abuse occurs. The fact that some people violate laws does not mean those laws should be eliminated.

Conclusion

Marriage stands at the center of human social organization, and the rules governing who may marry and in what numbers shape the fundamental structure of society. The case for maintaining strict criminalization of bigamy and polygamy rests not on prejudice or tradition but on clear-eyed analysis of what marriage is designed to accomplish and what happens when that design is departed from.

Marriage as an exclusive partnership between two people provides clarity of legal rights, protection for the most vulnerable, stability for children, and a framework for genuine consent that is impossible to achieve in polygamous arrangements. The historical record, contemporary evidence, and theoretical analysis all converge on the conclusion that polygamy produces systematic harm to women and children while undermining the social stability that marriage is meant to provide.

Those who would weaken restrictions on polygamy ask us to prioritize the preferences of a tiny minority over the wellbeing of women and children who would bear the consequences of such arrangements. They ask us to ignore centuries of accumulated wisdom about what makes for healthy families and stable societies. They ask us to pretend that consent can be meaningful in contexts of severe power imbalance and limited alternatives.

A society that truly values individual freedom, gender equality, and child welfare will maintain clear boundaries around marriage, preserving it as the exclusive partnership of two people that has proven most capable of serving these fundamental goods. The criminalization of bigamy and polygamy is not an imposition on liberty but rather a necessary protection for those who might otherwise be harmed by arrangements that wear the mask of choice while perpetuating structures of domination and exploitation.

The Criminalization of Bigamy and Polygamy: Rationales and Perceived Benefits

The legal prohibition of bigamy and polygamy represents one of the more enduring features of marriage law across numerous jurisdictions worldwide. Historical and Legal Foundations

The criminalization of bigamy and polygamy has deep roots in Western legal tradition, tracing its lineage to canonical Christian doctrine that established monogamous marriage as the only legally and spiritually valid form of marital union. English common law treated bigamy as a crime against the sacred bonds of marriage, and this tradition migrated with colonial expansion to influence legal systems across the globe. The influence of Christianity on Western jurisprudence cannot be overstated in this context, as theological commitments to the indissolubility of marriage and the equality of spouses before God translated into legal frameworks that recognized only single-spouse unions.

Similarly, in the United Kingdom, the Marriage Act of 1949 maintains provisions against polygamous marriages, reflecting historical anxieties about colonial subjects bringing practices from their home countries to metropolitan centers.

Arguments Concerning Social Stability

Proponents of monogamy-focused marriage laws have long argued that limiting marriage to two-person unions serves essential functions in maintaining social order and facilitating effective governance. The central contention here is that monogamous marriage creates clear, bounded family units that can be easily mapped onto legal and administrative systems, from inheritance laws to welfare distribution to criminal responsibility.

The clarity argument holds significant appeal for legal theorists who value predictability and administrability in law. When each individual possesses at most one recognized spouse, questions of property division upon death, eligibility for spousal benefits, and the determination of next-of-kin for medical decisions become relatively straightforward. Introducing plural spouses into these calculations creates what proponents describe as unnecessary complexity and potential for conflict. Courts would need to determine the relative rights of multiple spouses, allocate assets among multiple families, and adjudicate competing claims to legal standing—all while navigating emotionally charged disputes that already strain familial relationships.

Beyond administrative concerns, advocates for monogamy laws argue that such restrictions promote social cohesion by establishing a common institutional framework that unites disparate members of society. Marriage, in this view, functions as a social technology that connects individuals across different backgrounds and creates bonds of affinity that transcend kinship ties. When everyone participates in the same basic form of marital union, the theory suggests, society benefits from a shared understanding of family obligations and interpersonal commitments. Plural marriages, according to this perspective, might create insular units that resist integration into broader social structures, particularly when religious or cultural practices associated with polygamy mark practitioners as distinct from mainstream society.

The stability argument also extends to considerations of community welfare and social trust. Anthropological research in societies that permit plural marriage has documented tensions between co-wives and their respective children, competition for resources and spousal attention, and complications in inheritance that can generate long-lasting resentments. The protection of children provides perhaps the most emotionally compelling argument within this category. While causation remains difficult to establish and critics note that many such studies fail to control for confounding factors like poverty and social stigma, the concern for child welfare has nonetheless informed legislative responses to plural marriage. Additionally, the occasional discovery of abuse or neglect within insular polygamous communities has reinforced public perception that such arrangements create conditions conducive to the victimization of minors.

Religious and cultural communities that practice plural marriage contest these characterizations vigorously, arguing that their family structures provide healthy, supportive environments for children and that state intervention often causes more harm than it prevents. Nevertheless, the protective rationale continues to resonate with legislators and courts who view their role as safeguarding those unable to protect themselves.

Arguments Concerning Traditional and Religious Values

The traditional values argument for monogamy laws operates on multiple levels, invoking both secular traditions of Western jurisprudence and religious convictions about the proper form of marital union. While secular liberal democracies have grown increasingly uncomfortable with explicit appeals to religious doctrine in public policy, the historical influence of Christian marriage traditions on legal systems ensures that these arguments continue to shape debates about marriage reform.

The continuity argument holds that monogamous marriage has functioned as a foundational institution of Western civilization for millennia, providing the social architecture within which generations have been raised, property has been transmitted, and communities have sustained themselves. This perspective treats monogamy not as one possible arrangement among many but as the form of marriage that has proven itself through historical experience, cultivating the virtues of fidelity, mutual sacrifice, and long-term commitment that sustain healthy societies. Changing the legal definition of marriage to accommodate alternatives, including polygamy, would represent a radical departure from this accumulated wisdom about human flourishing.

Religious arguments for monogamy draw on scriptural and theological sources that establish the two-person marriage as divine ordinance. The Genesis account of Adam and Eve, interpreted through Christian theology, establishes a pattern in which marriage properly joins one man and one woman in a union that reflects the relationship between Christ and the Church. This theological framework treats monogamous marriage as more than a social convention; it constitutes a sacred institution whose alteration would violate divine will and spiritual order. From this perspective, laws against polygamy serve not merely as regulations of social behavior but as protections of holy ordinance.

The traditional values argument has grown more contested as societies have become pluralistic and as alternative family arrangements have gained social acceptance. Critics observe that appeals to tradition often function to legitimate existing power arrangements and that historical practices were frequently unjust in ways that tradition-minded defenders prefer to overlook. Furthermore, the association of monogamy with Western Christian civilization has acquired uncomfortable connotations in post-colonial contexts, where such arguments can appear as tools of cultural imperialism that impose European norms on societies with different marital traditions.

The rationales examined above represent perspectives that have influenced law and policy, but they exist within a broader debate in which many scholars and practitioners challenge their validity, their application, or their compatibility with fundamental principles of individual liberty and religious freedom.

The liberty critique holds that consenting adults should be free to structure their intimate relationships as they see fit, without state interference grounded in moral disapproval. Criminal liability recognizes that knowingly creating overlapping marital obligations is not simply a private disagreement. Prohibiting polygamy also protects equality within marriage. The more dependents one individual commands, the more difficult it may become for any one spouse to object, negotiate, or leave.

1. Marriage as a Legal Contract in Its Most Functional Form

1.1 The Marriage Contract as a Unitary Covenant

A marriage contract is a unitary covenant: it binds exactly two individuals together and, through that bond, establishes rights and duties that are indivisible. When a person contracts to be married to a second partner before dissolving the first, the fundamental contractual premise is violated. The legal guarantees afforded to spouses—rights to spousal support, healthcare decision‑making authority, inheritance rights, and tax benefits—are designed around a binary relationship. 2. Protecting the Rights and Integrity of Children

2.1 Legal Clarity in Custodial Rights

Children born into a polygamous family can find themselves subjected to disputes over custody and parental responsibilities. In the United States, the Supreme Court has held that child support payments must be “primarily paid to the Custodian of the Child" (McCarty v. County of Alameda). Multiple authoritative marital partners can create psychological confusion for children, especially when the parents' authority varies or alternates. Research has found increased incidence of anxiety, depression, and behavioral problems in children raised in polygamous families relative to those in monogamous families. Evidence indicates that stable parental unions predict better educational outcomes and reduced delinquency rates.

3.1 Coercion and Unequal Negotiation Power

Strong evidence demonstrates that polygamous marriages often involve coercive sexual practices, especially in cultures where the husband’s power dominates. Criminalizing bigamy protects vulnerable spouses—particularly women—who lack the equal bargaining power present in monogamous contexts. By limiting polygamous marriages, the law protects those individuals from potential abuse and psychological harm.

3.2 Protecting ‘Consent’ in Genuine Partnerships

A legally acknowledged marriage embodies the free consent of both parties. Bigamy disrupts the ability of spouses to willingly endorse another simultaneous marital relationship without the original partner’s knowledge. Evidently, civil law requires that a party's free will is exercised with full transparency regarding existing marital commitments.

4. Societal and Economic Costs

4.1 Bureaucratic Inefficiency

Every additional marital tie necessitates more sophisticated administrative frameworks for property settlement, pensions, pension revocation, etc. Historically, societies that practiced polygamy built separate legal categories for kinship evaluation, tax codes, inheritance, and benefit distribution. These complexities were far more costly and yielded less efficient resource use than a singular marital pathway.

4.2 Social Cohesion

Social science indicates that monogamous marriage fosters social cohesion by signaling stable and predictable communal structures. Polygamous unions, when widespread, can lead to a perception that property and social status are unevenly distributed, heightening jealousy or envy within communities, as evidenced in colonial studies in the Southern United States.

The United Nations recommends protecting “the rights of spouses, children, and minors” and recognizes the sanctity of marriage. 5.2 Secular Humanism

Secular states align marriage with universal human rights, most importantly the right to a dignified, stable family life. Under this lens, any practice altering a marriage's exclusive nature threatens the moral framework of society.

Marriage stands as a critical institution combining love, mutual commitment, the raising of children, and financial stewardship. The Case for Preserving Monogamous Marriage: Why Bigamy and Polygamy Should Remain Criminal Offenses

Introduction

Marriage stands as one of society's most fundamental institutions, serving as the bedrock upon which families are built and communities flourish. Throughout much of the modern world, this institution has been defined as an exclusive partnership between two individuals—a definition that deserves vigorous legal protection. While some advocate for the decriminalization or acceptance of bigamy and polygamy, compelling legal, social, and practical reasons demand that we maintain and enforce strict prohibitions against multiple-partner marriages. The criminalization of bigamy and polygamy represents not an arbitrary restriction on personal freedom, but rather a necessary safeguard for individual rights, social stability, and the welfare of society's most vulnerable members.

The Legal Framework: Protecting Individual Rights and Preventing Exploitation

The legal prohibition of bigamy and polygamy serves crucial protective functions within our justice system. Marriage confers numerous legal rights and responsibilities—from inheritance and medical decision-making to tax benefits and immigration status. When marriage involves only two parties, these rights remain clear and enforceable. Multiple-partner marriages, however, create legal quagmires that can leave individuals vulnerable to exploitation and abuse.

Consider the practical implications: In a polygamous arrangement, how are social security benefits divided? Who has medical decision-making authority when spouses disagree? How are custody arrangements determined when multiple adults claim parental rights? The bilateral nature of monogamous marriage provides clear answers to these questions, protecting both parties' interests equally. Polygamous arrangements, by contrast, create hierarchies and power imbalances that the law cannot adequately address without fundamentally restructuring our entire legal system.

Furthermore, the criminalization of bigamy protects unwitting individuals from fraud. Cases abound of individuals who discover their spouse has another family, leaving them emotionally devastated and legally compromised. Criminal sanctions against bigamy provide recourse for these victims and deter would-be perpetrators from engaging in such deceptive practices.

Safeguarding Gender Equality and Women's Rights

Historical and contemporary evidence demonstrates that polygamous societies consistently exhibit greater gender inequality than monogamous ones. While polygamy theoretically could involve multiple husbands or gender-neutral arrangements, in practice, it overwhelmingly manifests as polygyny—one man with multiple wives. This structure inherently creates power imbalances that subordinate women.

In polygamous arrangements, women often compete for resources and attention from a shared husband, undermining solidarity and mutual support among women. Young women in particular face pressure to enter polygamous marriages with older, established men, limiting their educational and professional opportunities. The practice frequently correlates with earlier marriage ages for girls, higher maternal mortality rates, and reduced female participation in public life.

Monogamous marriage, while not immune to gender-based problems, provides a structural foundation for equality between partners. Each spouse holds equal legal status, and neither can unilaterally alter the fundamental nature of the relationship by adding additional partners. This equality under law represents a crucial achievement in the advancement of women's rights that polygamy inherently undermines.

Protecting Children's Welfare

Research consistently indicates that children thrive best in stable, two-parent households where both parents can devote substantial time and resources to child-rearing. Polygamous families, by contrast, often struggle with resource dilution—both financial and emotional. When parental attention must be divided among multiple spouses and larger numbers of children, individual children receive less support and guidance.

Studies of polygamous communities reveal concerning patterns: higher rates of poverty, reduced educational achievement, and increased behavioral problems among children. The complex family dynamics in polygamous households—including rivalry between different mothers' children and unclear authority structures—create environments prone to conflict and instability.

Moreover, the criminalization of polygamy helps prevent the isolation of children in closed communities where educational opportunities may be limited and where young people, particularly girls, may face pressure to enter plural marriages themselves. By maintaining clear legal standards for marriage, society better protects children's rights to education, healthcare, and freedom of choice in their own future relationships.

Preserving Social Cohesion and Democratic Values

Monogamous marriage promotes social stability and cohesion in ways that polygamous structures cannot replicate. In societies where monogamy is the norm, marriage creates bonds between families and communities, weaving a social fabric of interconnected relationships. Each marriage links two family networks, creating broader social connections and mutual obligations.

Polygamous societies, conversely, tend toward concentration of power and resources. Wealthy or powerful men accumulate multiple wives, leaving many lower-status men without marriage prospects. This imbalance breeds resentment, social instability, and violence. Historical analysis reveals that polygamous societies experience higher rates of crime, political instability, and authoritarian governance.

Furthermore, monogamous marriage aligns with democratic principles of equality and individual rights. Just as each citizen receives one vote, each person can enter into one marriage partnership. This egalitarian approach to marriage reflects and reinforces broader democratic values, while polygamy's inherent inequalities contradict these fundamental principles.

Economic Considerations: Preventing Fraud and Protecting Public Resources

The economic implications of decriminalizing bigamy and polygamy extend far beyond individual households. Our tax system, social welfare programs, and employee benefit structures all assume monogamous marriage. Allowing polygamous marriages would require massive restructuring of these systems, potentially creating opportunities for fraud and abuse.

Consider employer-provided health insurance: Should companies be required to cover multiple spouses? How would this impact healthcare costs and employment practices? Similarly, immigration laws granting spousal visas assume one spouse per citizen. Polygamous arrangements could be exploited for immigration fraud, undermining the integrity of our immigration system.

The criminalization of bigamy and polygamy prevents these economic complications while protecting public resources from potential abuse. It maintains clear boundaries that allow our economic and social systems to function efficiently and fairly.

Addressing Counterarguments: Why Personal Freedom Has Limits

Advocates for decriminalizing polygamy often invoke arguments about personal freedom and consenting adults' right to structure their relationships as they choose. The freedom to enter exploitative or harmful arrangements is not a freedom worth protecting.

Moreover, true consent in polygamous relationships is often questionable. In communities where polygamy is practiced, young women may face enormous social, economic, and religious pressure to enter such arrangements. The power dynamics inherent in polygamous relationships can make genuine, ongoing consent difficult to ensure or verify.

International Perspectives: Learning from Global Experience

The international trend moves decisively toward monogamous marriage. Countries that have modernized their legal systems consistently prohibit polygamy, recognizing its incompatibility with gender equality and human rights. The United Nations Human Rights Committee has stated that polygamy violates the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, as it discriminates against women.

Nations that have attempted to accommodate polygamy within modern legal frameworks have struggled with intractable problems. No country has successfully created a legal system that allows polygamy while maintaining gender equality, children's rights, and social stability. This global experience reinforces the wisdom of maintaining criminal prohibitions against bigamy and polygamy.

Conclusion

The criminalization of bigamy and polygamy represents not an archaic restriction on personal freedom, but a necessary foundation for a just and stable society. By preserving marriage as an exclusive partnership between two individuals, we protect individual rights, promote gender equality, safeguard children's welfare, and maintain social cohesion. Some boundaries exist for good reasons, protecting vulnerable individuals and preserving social goods that benefit everyone. The prohibition against bigamy and polygamy is one such boundary—a legal standard that upholds human dignity, promotes equality, and protects the institution of marriage itself.

Our commitment to monogamous marriage reflects our deeper commitment to human equality, individual rights, and social justice. By maintaining and enforcing laws against bigamy and polygamy, we affirm these values and protect them for future generations. In a world of rapid social change, some principles deserve not reconsideration but renewed commitment. The exclusive, monogamous nature of marriage is one such principle—a cornerstone of civilized society that we abandon at our peril.

Introduction

Marriage is one of the most sacred and foundational institutions in human society. Human beings are not the only species that practice monogamy—approximately 3-5% of mammal species (including gibbons, beavers, and some primates) form lifelong pair bonds.   • Jealousy and mate guarding are universal human traits that evolved to prevent infidelity and ensure exclusive partnerships, further supporting monogamy as the natural state.

While some argue that polygyny (one man, multiple wives) was historically common, this was often not a matter of choice but of power dynamics, where wealthy or powerful men could afford multiple wives while the majority of men remained monogamous or unmarried.   • **Even in countries where polygamy is culturally practiced (e.g., parts of Africa and the Middle East), it is often not legally recognized or severely restricted.

The global consensus is clear: monogamy is the only acceptable form of marriage.

A. Bigamy Must Remain a Crime to Prevent Fraud and Deception

Bigamy is not just a moral issue—it is a legal one, as it involves fraud, financial exploitation, and deception.

  • **A bigamous marriage is a criminal offense because it deprives the first spouse of legal rights (e.g., inheritance, social benefits, custody).

  • Divorce rates would skyrocket as people seek "better" partners while still legally married to others.
  • Societal trust in institutions would erode, as people would no longer believe in the permanence of marriage.

Monogamy is the only way to uphold the sanctity of marriage.

Conclusion: Monogamy Must Remain the Only Legally Recognized Form of Marriage

The case for strict criminalization of bigamy and polygamy is overwhelming. Monogamy is biologically, psychologically, and socially the most stable foundation for marriage, while polygamy leads to exploitation, inequality, and instability. Historical, religious, and legal traditions overwhelmingly support monogamy, and modern societies must uphold this standard to protect individuals, families, and society as a whole.

The Case for Strict Criminalization of Bigamy and Polygamy: Why Marriage Must Remain an Exclusive Bond Between Two People

Introduction

Marriage, as a foundational social institution, shapes the structure of families, communities, and the legal frameworks that govern property, inheritance, parental rights, and the welfare of children. Across the vast majority of human civilizations and legal systems, marriage has been understood as an exclusive, monogamous partnership between two individuals. The criminalization of bigamy—entering into a marriage while already legally married to another person—and polygamy—maintaining multiple simultaneous marriages—is not an arbitrary restriction on personal freedom but a vital safeguard of social order, gender equality, and human dignity. Strict enforcement of monogamy laws remains necessary, and the arguments for decriminalization are weaker than they appear when subjected to rigorous scrutiny.

Legal Clarity and Institutional Integrity

The legal definition of marriage as a two-person union is not a mere convention; it is the cornerstone of family law. When states issue marriage licenses, they create a dyadic legal relationship with clearly defined rights and obligations: spousal support, property division, inheritance rights, decision-making authority, and next-of-kin status. Multiplying the parties involved transforms this elegant, workable framework into an unmanageable tangle.

Consider the legal questions that arise: If a man has three wives, what happens when he divorces one? Do the other wives have a claim on the marital property allocated to her? In cases of abuse, which spouse has standing to file for protective orders? If one wife bears a child, do all three wives have parental rights? These are not hypothetical complications; they are predictable consequences of legalizing plural marriage. The American Bar Association and virtually every legal scholar who has examined the issue has noted that plural marriage creates irresolvable conflicts of interest that existing legal structures cannot accommodate.

The Historical Record of Harm

One cannot seriously discuss polygamy without confronting its documented consequences. In societies and communities that have practiced plural marriage—whether the Mormon fundamentalist sects of the American West, the practices documented in parts of the Middle East and Africa, or isolated cases elsewhere—the pattern of harm is consistent and damning.

Polygamous communities consistently show:

  • Higher rates of domestic violence against women, who are often isolated and lack the social power to escape abusive situations
  • Disproportionate suffering for first wives and childless wives, who are frequently displaced as younger women are added to the household
  • Lower educational outcomes and economic opportunities for girls, who are often married off young to older men with multiple wives
  • A statistical correlation with poverty, welfare dependency, and reduced female autonomy
  • Documented cases of child abuse, including child trafficking and child labor, in underground polygamous communities that arise to evade the law

These are not incidental features that can be reformed away. They are structural consequences of a system that inherently subordinates women, commodifies marriage, and creates incentives for the marginalization of some members of the family unit.

Protection of the Vulnerable

Perhaps the most compelling argument for criminalization is the protection of women and children, who are overwhelmingly the victims when plural marriage is practiced. In the rare communities where polygamy has been practiced openly or semi-openly, the demographic pattern is unmistakable: a small number of older, wealthier men accumulating multiple younger wives, while the rest of the male population is structurally excluded from marriage.

This creates a society of haves and have-nots, with the dispossessed young men and the trapped young women both suffering. A 25-year-old woman "married" to a 50-year-old man with three other wives has not made a free choice in any meaningful sense; she has been absorbed into a system that limits her alternatives from birth. Strict criminalization of polygamy provides law enforcement with tools to intervene before girls are coerced into marriage, before young women are trafficked between communities, and before abusive husbands use the cover of plural marriage to shield their crimes.

The argument that adult women freely choose polygamy is, in the real-world cases we have observed, largely fictional. Choice requires alternatives, and the structure of polygamous communities systematically eliminates them.

Preventing Fraud and Protecting the Public

Bigamy is not a victimless crime. When a person enters into a marriage while already legally married, they defraud their new spouse of the most basic assumption of marriage: that it is exclusive. The "second spouse" has been lied to about a foundational fact of their relationship. This is genuine harm, both emotional and material—he or she may have given up career opportunities, relocated, had children, and built an entire life under false pretenses.

Moreover, bigamy frequently accompanies other crimes: immigration fraud, financial fraud, insurance fraud, and sexual assault. The men who pursue multiple wives are often the same men who use deception, manipulation, and coercion to build their "families." Criminalization of bigamy gives prosecutors a tool to address this conduct directly, rather than requiring them to charge the peripheral crimes while the underlying pattern continues unabated.

Social Stability and Child Welfare

Children raised in monogamous two-parent households have, on average and across virtually every measurable outcome, better life chances than children in any other family configuration. This is not a moral judgment; it is a statistical reality supported by decades of social science research. While single parents and other family structures can and do raise healthy, successful children, the data on the two-parent, monogamous family as the most stable environment for child development is remarkably consistent.

Polygamous families, by contrast, introduce instability, rivalry among half-siblings, divided parental attention, and frequent family dissolution when the patriarch's resources are stretched too thin or when conflict arises between co-wives. Children in such families often experience identity confusion, loyalty conflicts, and economic insecurity. Strict criminalization of polygamy is, in this sense, a child welfare policy.

The Religious Liberty Argument Refuted

Defenders of polygamy often invoke religious liberty, pointing to historical Mormon polygamy, certain Islamic traditions, or isolated African practices. But religious freedom in the American system—and in most constitutional democracies—has never been unlimited. The Free Exercise Clause does not protect practices that harm others, defraud the public, or undermine civil institutions. Courts have consistently upheld laws against human sacrifice, drug use, and yes, plural marriage, on precisely these grounds.

No serious theologian, regardless of tradition, argues that religious liberty requires the state to recognize or facilitate relationships that systematically subordinate half of the faithful. The Catholic Church, the Eastern Orthodox Church, most Protestant denominations, mainstream Sunni and Shia Islam, Orthodox Judaism, and virtually every other major religious body officially endorses monogamy. The "religious liberty" argument for polygamy is, in practice, the liberty of a small fringe to impose its practices on vulnerable members of its own community.

The Personal Autonomy Argument Refuted

A more sophisticated case for decriminalization invokes personal autonomy: if three or more adults wish to form a family together, why should the state prevent them? The answer is that the state is not preventing private relationships, unusual household arrangements, or even complex romantic entanglements. The state is refusing to extend a specific legal status—marriage—that carries hundreds of specific legal consequences—to a configuration that cannot accommodate them.

Moreover, the autonomy argument ignores the children, the extended families, and the surrounding community that are also affected when plural marriage is recognized. Marriage is not a private contract like a cell phone plan; it is a public institution with public consequences. Society has a legitimate interest in maintaining its foundational definitions.

Conclusion

Strict criminalization of bigamy and polygamy is not an antiquated holdover from a more puritanical era. It is a deliberate, necessary, and defensible policy choice that protects the integrity of marriage, safeguards vulnerable women and children, maintains workable legal frameworks, and preserves social stability. The voices calling for decriminalization are, in practice, voices defending arrangements that have demonstrably harmed the people most subject to them.

Monogamous marriage is not a perfect institution, and it can be the site of abuse, infidelity, and dysfunction. But it remains the family structure most compatible with gender equality, child welfare, and the rule of law. Policymakers should resist the temptation to relax these laws in the name of tolerance or inclusivity. The price of doing so will be paid by women and children who lack the resources to protect themselves.

Marriage must remain, as it has been for most of human history and across the great majority of human civilizations, an exclusive partnership between two individuals. Anything else is not progress—it is regression into a system that history has repeatedly shown to be incompatible with human dignity and equality.

A note on intellectual honesty: This essay represents one side of an active debate. Reasonable people, including some feminists, legal scholars, and members of polyamorous communities, argue that decriminalization—with appropriate safeguards—could allow better regulation and protection of those already practicing plural marriage. Readers should weigh the arguments on both sides thoughtfully.

Arguments for Criminalizing Bigamy and Polygamy

Laws against bigamy (marrying one person while already married to another) and polygamy (having multiple spouses simultaneously) exist in many jurisdictions, particularly in Western legal traditions. The following outlines the main rationales commonly cited for these prohibitions.

1. Historical and Legal Foundations

Most Western legal systems inherited prohibitions on plural marriage from English common law, canon law, and later statutory frameworks such as England's Bigamy Act of 1604 and the Morrill Anti-Bigamy Act (1862) in the United States. These laws were reinforced by:

  • Christian theological tradition, which elevated monogamy as a moral ideal.
  • Colonial legal codes that imposed monogamous marriage norms on diverse populations.
  • Republican civic ideology, particularly in the U.S., which viewed monogamous marriage as compatible with democratic citizenship.

2. Social Stability

Proponents argue that monogamous marriage supports social order in several ways:

  • Demographic predictability: A one-to-one spousal model simplifies inheritance, citizenship, lineage, and household composition, reducing disputes over resources and status.
  • Equal adult ratios: Polygyny (one man, multiple wives) is argued by some scholars to create shortages of eligible women, potentially leading to increased competition, social friction, and even violence among unmarried men. The "marriage squeeze" hypothesis has been cited in studies of societies with high polygyny rates.
  • Reduced factionalism: Some argue that extended polygamous networks can entrench wealth concentration and political cliques, while monogamy disperses social ties more broadly.
  • Child welfare continuity: A two-parent structure is said to provide more stable attachment figures, though this claim is contested by researchers who note that quality of relationships matters more than quantity of parents.

3. Preventing Exploitation

A central argument in modern legal and feminist critique is that polygamous systems enable exploitation, particularly of women and girls:

  • Unequal power dynamics: Critics argue that in many polygamous communities, first wives often have diminished status once subsequent wives are introduced, with reduced economic and emotional security.
  • Coerced consent: Studies of polygynous communities, including exit-cult accounts and legal proceedings, describe young women being married to older men, sometimes under family or religious pressure, with limited recourse.
  • Underage marriage: Polygamy is associated in some documented cases with child marriage, which is independently illegal in most jurisdictions.
  • Limited exit options: Leaving a polygamous household can mean losing children, housing, and community standing, effectively trapping individuals—especially women—in unwanted arrangements.
  • Immigration and trafficking concerns: Several countries have used anti-polygamy laws to combat coerced marriage and trafficking schemes.

4. Upholding Traditional and Civic Values
